High volume, high frequency — and a high recovery bill

6-Day Workout Split: PPL, Arnold Split and Heavy/Light Options

Short answer: Push/pull/legs run twice a week is the standard 6-day split, giving every muscle two sessions. The Arnold split is a higher-volume alternative for experienced lifters.

How a 6-day workout split works

A six-day split is a commitment to training nearly every day. Done well, it gives each muscle two weekly sessions and enough total volume to keep advanced lifters progressing. Done poorly, it is a fast route to fatigue.

The key is that six hard sessions are not required — many lifters run a 6-day structure with a deliberate mix of heavy and lighter days so that fatigue does not accumulate.

Best 6-day split structures

Push / Pull / Legs ×2 (recommended)

MonPush
TuePull
WedLegs
ThuPush
FriPull
SatLegs
SunRest

Best for: Intermediate to advanced lifters who recover well. Each muscle twice a week with clear separation.

Trade-off: Legs twice a week plus pulling twice puts real demand on your lower back and grip across the week.

Arnold Split

MonChest & Back
TueShoulders & Arms
WedLegs
ThuChest & Back
FriShoulders & Arms
SatLegs
SunRest

Best for: Experienced lifters who like antagonist pairings and high-volume training.

Trade-off: Chest & back sessions are long. It is demanding and usually not a first choice for newer lifters.

Load this in the planner →

Heavy / Light PPL

MonPush (heavy)
TuePull (heavy)
WedLegs (heavy)
ThuPush (light)
FriPull (light)
SatLegs (light)
SunRest

Best for: Lifters who want PPL volume but need to manage fatigue. First half of the week is heavy; second is lighter and higher-rep.

Trade-off: Requires honest self-regulation — light days really have to be light.

Is a 6-day split right for you?

Beginner friendlyLow
Muscle buildingExcellent for advanced lifters
StrengthGood — depends on how heavy the main lifts are
Schedule flexibilityLow
Recovery demandVery high
Session length60–90 min
Weekly frequency per muscle2×

Pros

  • Twice-weekly frequency for every muscle
  • High weekly volume potential
  • Short breaks between muscle groups
  • Predictable structure

Cons

  • Very demanding on recovery, sleep and nutrition
  • Little room for life disruptions
  • Easy to accumulate fatigue and stall
  • Not necessary for most people

Best for

  • Experienced lifters with solid recovery
  • People who enjoy daily training and have the time
  • Lifters who have outgrown 4–5 day plans

Think twice if…

  • Beginners
  • People with limited sleep, high stress or physically demanding jobs
  • Anyone who regularly misses sessions

Recovery is the whole game

With one rest day a week, recovery has to be managed inside the plan: vary intensity between the two cycles, limit sets taken to failure, and keep total sets per muscle in a reasonable range.

Watch for the usual warning signs — falling performance, persistent soreness, poor sleep, low motivation. If they appear, drop a day or run a lighter week rather than pushing on.

6-day workout split FAQ

Is a 6-day workout split good?

It can be for experienced lifters who recover well. For most people, four or five days produces similar results with less fatigue.

PPL or Arnold on six days?

PPL is simpler and easier to progress. The Arnold split trains more muscles per session and suits experienced lifters who like higher volume.

How do I avoid burnout on a 6-day plan?

Use heavy and light days, keep most sets short of failure, schedule a deload week every 6–8 weeks, and take your rest day seriously.
